transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, nice to meet you too. Um... I guess I'm here because people keep telling me I'm not listening to them. 

Like my supervisor at work, or my wife. They'll be talking straight to me, and... I don't know, a minute later I realize I only caught half of what they said. Then I end up having to ask them to say it again. So... yeah. That's mainly it.
When people are talking to you, do the words ever sound clear but still not make sense right away?
Uh... no, I don't think so. It's not that it doesn't make sense. I hear the words fine, I just... I'm just not listening, I guess.
Do you remember having the same kind of trouble paying attention when you were a child, like in grade school?

Yeah... I guess I was like this back then, too. 

Um, I remember teachers were always moving my desk. Said I couldn't stay in my seat. And, uh... I used to just blurt out answers a lot. Got in trouble for messing with other kids' stuff, too, before I even hit middle school. So, yeah. I guess it's been a while.
Do these attention problems also cause trouble for you outside of work, like at home?

Yeah... I guess so. At home, uh... my wife and kids get pretty frustrated with me. I guess I kind of disrupt the routines instead of helping things run smooth. 

And it's... it's getting bad at work, too. I've actually had a few formal warnings. Working the line, you know... I worry I'm gonna cause a safety problem or just... lose my job over it. So, yeah. It causes trouble.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes persistent inattentive symptoms (not listening when spoken to) with corroborating childhood history of hyperactive/impulsive behaviors (could not stay seated, blurting out answers, interfering with others' belongings) beginning before middle school and continuing into adulthood. Symptoms are present across settings (work and home) and are causing clear functional impairment, including family conflict, formal work warnings, and concern about workplace safety. No evidence in the interview suggests a primary language comprehension problem or another better explanation.
